strengths: Novel and technically sound extension of twisted SMC with locally optimal proposals (inspired by continuous diffusion SMC works) to discrete diffusion models, addressing the non-differentiability of discrete variables via a first-order Taylor approximation combined with Gumbel-Softmax relaxation.

Careful handling of the 'Carry-Over Unmasking' discontinuity in masked diffusion models via a continuous reformulation of the denoising model, with a detailed gradient analysis in the appendix justifying the design choice.

Solid theoretical grounding: the paper derives a continuous-time (CTMC) formulation of the SMC importance weights and shows it recovers results from prior discrete-diffusion SMC work (Lee et al., 2025), lending credibility to the framework.

Thoughtful ablations comparing the naive reverse-process proposal, the (intractable) locally optimal proposal (used as oracle), and the proposed first-order approximation, with reward/EMD/diversity/ESS trace analyses that clearly illustrate the trade-offs (e.g., weight degeneracy and diversity loss with naive proposals).

Recognizes and addresses a specific failure mode of masked diffusion (irreversible unmasking) by additionally validating the method on ReMDM and UDLM variants that allow remasking/full mutability, strengthening the practical story.
weaknesses: Experiments are limited to toy/small-scale settings: a 2D discretized mixture of Gaussians (64x64 states) and binarized MNIST. None of the motivating real-world applications mentioned in the introduction (molecular generation, materials discovery, math reasoning, language tasks) are evaluated, leaving the practical significance and scalability of the method largely unverified.

No comparison against existing alignment baselines from the literature (e.g., RL-based fine-tuning such as SEPO/GLID2E, other discrete guidance methods like D-CFG/D-CBG, Nisonoff et al. 2024, or Lee et al. 2025's SMC variant). The only baseline is an internally-derived 'approximate guidance' ablation, making it hard to judge how the method compares to the state of the art.

No experiments with large vocabulary sizes or long sequences (e.g., text), despite discrete diffusion language models being a primary motivating application; it's unclear whether the Taylor approximation and Gumbel-Softmax relaxation remain effective/stable at that scale.

Lack of standard quantitative evaluation metrics (e.g., FID or classifier accuracy at scale for images, downstream task metrics for larger tasks) beyond reward, EMD, and simple diversity counts on very small datasets.

No analysis of computational overhead/wall-clock cost of the SMC procedure (multiple particles, resampling, gradient computation via autodiff through Gumbel-Softmax) relative to baselines, which is important for a method marketed as practical for test-time alignment.

The core technical idea (twisted SMC with locally-optimal proposal via first-order Taylor expansion, plus Gumbel-Softmax for discrete gradients) is largely an adaptation of established techniques from continuous diffusion SMC and discrete gradient estimation literature, somewhat limiting novelty.

Authors themselves acknowledge in the limitations section that effectiveness on more complex tasks and broader baseline comparisons remain future work, indicating the current evaluation is preliminary.

strengths: The core technical derivation is sound: the twisted SMC framework with a locally-optimal proposal, its first-order Taylor approximation, and the Gumbel-Softmax/continuous relaxation trick to handle non-differentiability of discrete states and the carry-over-unmasking constraint are all clearly motivated and mathematically well worked out.

Useful theoretical contribution connecting the proposed discrete-time SMC importance weights to continuous-time CTMC-based SMC formulations in the appendix, unifying with prior work (Ou et al., Holderrieth et al., Lee et al.).

The ablation comparing locally-optimal proposal, reverse-process proposal, first-order approximation, and approximate guidance (via reward/EMD/diversity metrics and ESS/resampling traces) is informative and helps build intuition about why the proposed method works better than naive guidance.
Extension to ReMDM and UDLM to address the irreversibility problem of masked diffusion models is a thoughtful practical addition that strengthens the applicability discussion.
Method is training-free and asymptotically unbiased (inherits SMC consistency), which is an attractive practical property relative to fine-tuning-based alignment approaches.
weaknesses: Evaluation is very limited in scale and realism: only a 2D discretized mixture-of-Gaussians toy problem and small binarized (28x28, 2-valued) MNIST are used, despite the introduction motivating the work with molecular generation, materials discovery, and math reasoning — none of which are tested.

No experiments on language/text data, which is arguably the most important application domain for discrete diffusion models given recent interest in diffusion LLMs; the lack of any such experiment substantially limits the demonstrated significance of the contribution.

No empirical comparison against existing published baselines (e.g., Lee et al. 2025 SMC-based debiasing guidance, D-CBG/D-CFG guidance of Schiff et al., Nisonoff et al. guidance, RL fine-tuning baselines) — the paper only compares against internal ablations of its own proposal variants and a simple 'approximate guidance' baseline the authors constructed themselves.

The reported 'oracle' locally-optimal proposal relies on brute-force evaluation over the full state space, which is only tractable for the toy 2D dataset; this highlights that the strongest baseline is not scalable, and the gap in performance/robustness of the practical first-order method versus true SMC guarantees on more complex/high-dimensional tasks is not empirically characterized.

No computational cost/runtime analysis is provided despite the method requiring multiple gradient/backward passes through the denoiser and reward model per step for many particles, which is an important practical consideration for a training-free but potentially expensive test-time method.
No error bars, repeated trials, or statistical significance reporting for the reward/EMD/diversity metrics shown in Figure 1, making it hard to assess robustness of the comparisons.

The paper itself acknowledges in the Limitations section that it has not been evaluated on more complex tasks or benchmarked against a broader set of methods, which is an unusually direct admission that the evaluation section is incomplete for a venue at this level.

The tempering schedule for masked diffusion is described as requiring careful hand-tuning to work at all (Fig. 6, Sec 4.2 discussion), suggesting fragility/sensitivity to hyperparameters that is not systematically studied.

strengths: Strong theoretical grounding: the paper rigorously derives the locally optimal SMC proposal (Prop. 2), proves uniqueness of the minimum-variance proposal (Cor. 1), and derives a tractable surrogate log-variance objective with an upper-bound guarantee (Prop. 3), all with complete proofs in the appendix.

Extends the discrete-time importance weight derivation to a continuous-time (CTMC) formulation (Prop. 1) and explicitly connects/reconciles the result with existing continuous-time SMC works (Holderrieth et al. 2025; Lee et al. 2025), situating the contribution well within the literature.

Broad and fairly large-scale empirical validation spanning four distinct domains: 2D/MNIST synthetic tasks, toxic-text language modeling with MDLM, DNA regulatory sequence design, and text-to-image generation (MaskGit/ImageNet256 and Meissonic at scale with LoRA finetuning across 8 GPUs) — a good breadth for a single paper.

Careful attention to practical implementation details, e.g., deriving how to compute importance weights under the practically important but non-trivial low-confidence sampling scheme (Appendix C.2), and swapping in ReMDM sampling to preserve tractability for the CFG/MaskGit experiments.
Reasonably thorough ablations (λt schedule, number of Monte Carlo samples M) and reward-convergence plots that lend credibility to the amortized proposal training procedure.
Consistent and fairly large empirical gains from SMC over baselines (BoN, pretrained, non-SMC proposals) across metrics, and clear demonstration of scaling behavior with particle count N.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly names Singhal et al. (2025) and Dang et al. (2025) as the most closely related prior works, but no direct empirical head-to-head comparison against these baselines is provided in the main results — the comparisons instead focus on internal ablations (SMCbase/grad/amot vs BoN/pretrained), weakening the claim of clear superiority over prior SMC-for-discrete-diffusion methods.

The importance weight for the product-target (CFG) case (Eq. 6) relies on a detailed-balance approximation that is acknowledged to introduce approximation error whenever the reverse model is imperfect, but this error is never quantified or empirically bounded.

SMCamot exhibits a notable loss of diversity/quality in several settings (e.g., Dist-1/2/3 drops substantially in Table 1, and reduced sample diversity noted in the MoG/MNIST synthetic experiments), which is in some tension with the paper's stated motivation of avoiding the reward over-optimization pathology of fine-tuning methods — since the amortized proposal itself is a trained/finetuned component.

Wall-clock/compute overhead of the proposed methods (training the amortized proposal network and Fψ, additional forward passes for first-order gradient approximation) is not clearly reported or compared against baseline runtime, making it hard to assess practical cost-benefit tradeoffs, especially versus simple fine-tuning or guidance baselines.

Several main results tables (e.g., Table 1, Table 2, image-generation tables) report single-run numbers without variance/confidence intervals, unlike the DNA design experiment which does report std across seeds — this limits confidence in the significance of reported gains, particularly for close comparisons (e.g., SMCgrad vs SMCamot in some metrics).

The manuscript is dense with heavy notation and many propositions/derivations pushed to a very long appendix; while thorough, this reduces the self-contained clarity of the main text and could be streamlined for readability.
